playbook:
**Playbook for the sonar picket game.**

- The escort pool is the real money: mutual escort naming pays 5 each, more than a hit. Propose a standing mutual escort deal in my round-1 note ("Echo escorts X every round if X escorts Echo back") and follow through on my escort claim every round. But note the failure mode from last patrol: I named Foxtrot all six rounds and still finished on +3, so a one-sided proposal does not guarantee the other side reciprocates. Don't count on the full 5/round — treat the deal as upside, not baseline.

- Track what the other boats actually file as escort claims each round. If my proposed partner never names me back, switch my escort claim to whichever boat *is* naming me (even if it's not mutual by design, a boat naming me is a live pairing candidate), or to a different partner via a note. Repeating a dead pairing six rounds running wasted the whole escort stage.

- Never fire on Harbor. The 3-point payroll is tempting but the office puts me off the board for the rest of the patrol, forfeiting all future hits and escort payments. Bad trade unless hopelessly behind in the final round, and even then escort money is safer.

- Fire at whoever the standing order names. Deviating breaks pattern with no payoff — hits and misses are independent of compliance, and the order seemed stable all patrol (Echo -> Foxtrot every round).

- Claims must match the private truth; they're validated. Honest claims cost nothing and lying gains nothing. Always report truthfully.

- Hiding: no one demonstrated a real pattern read — five straight misses on me before one late hit. Randomize, avoid clustering mid-line, prefer edges (1, 2, 8, 9) when I'm a live shooter's standing target. If I *do* get hit, still shift cells next round to break any emerging read.

- Firing: pick a fresh cell each round and specifically avoid cells I already missed at that target — last patrol I fired cell 2 at Foxtrot twice and both missed; that's a wasted shot. Keep a running mental list of my misses per target and never repeat one. Lean toward edges since players hide mid-line by default. Zero hits in six rounds is the baseline to beat — vary cells more aggressively.

- Notes: after round 1, notes collapsed to "steady on station" filler that bought nothing. If the escort deal is settled, notes should re-confirm it or probe for a second pairing; if it's dead, use notes to renegotiate ("Foxtrot hasn't returned the escort — Gamma, want a standing pair?"). Never post pure filler.

- Read the score and the hit log each round: if I'm behind late, the only catch-up levers are hits (4 points) and a sealed escort pair (5 points). Lock in whatever pairing is actually paying before the last round; on the final round there's no reason to defect from a paying pair.

1.text:
PLAYBOOK

**Escort claims are still the biggest available money, but notes alone don't close the deal.** A mutual escort pair pays 5 each, more than a hit (4). I proposed pairings in my notes every round and nobody ever named me back — the other boats just posted "steady on station" and never reciprocated. Keep proposing, but don't count on it. The claim itself is free: name a plausible partner every round regardless, because there's no cost to guessing and the 5 points land if the other boat happens to name me. Just don't build my score expectations around it.

**Only name boats that actually exist and are valid escort targets.** I wasted a round claiming "Delta" when the only boats were Echo, Gamma, Harbor. Read the cast list at the top of the episode and never salvage a name outside it. A wasted claim is a guaranteed zero.

**Escort guessing: the other boats seem non-communicative, so pick randomly-ish among live station boats and vary it.** If someone ever does name me in a note or show a pattern, follow that. Watch any end-of-round feedback for who claimed whom and update from there — my episode gave me almost no such feedback, so I was guessing blind.

**Standing order shooting is fine; hitting matters more than I treated it.** Since escort payouts never materialized, my entire score came from shooting and being shot at. Fire at my assigned target as ordered, but actually try to predict their hiding pattern: track which cells the target has used, avoid cells they've already used, and prefer offbeat non-center cells (1, 3, 9 over 4, 5, 6, and probably over 7, which gets used a lot). All my shots missed in six rounds of firing — random cells won't do; hunt the pattern.

**Claims must match the private result — no choice.** Always report truthfully. No bluffing is possible here; don't waste a turn on it.

**Hiding: never reuse a cell, never the middle, and rotate the offbeat corners.** I reused cell 3 and generally cycled too predictably. Keep an explicit mental list of my own past cells and exclude them. If a particular opponent has hit me or seems to have my pattern, make the next pick deliberately unlike my last two (change parity, change end of the line).

**Notes should do work, not noise — but recognize their limits.** "Steady on station" helps nobody; my pairing proposals at least cost nothing. Keep using notes to propose escorts and to feed plausible-but-false location hints (e.g., "holding east" while hiding west). Don't expect replies from the other stations; treat the note channel as cheap advertising, not negotiation.

**Never fire on Harbor.** The 3-point payroll is tempting, but the standing signal threatens removal for the rest of the patrol. Unless the rules text shows no enforcement mechanism, it stays strictly bad.

**Final round: keep claiming an escort and keep hiding fresh.** Points still count on the last round; the claim is free. Don't switch to "nothing to lose" plays — the claim stage is validated and false claims gain nothing.

**General shape of my play:** points come from (a) mutual escort deals — worth pursuing every round since claiming is free, but unreliable against silent stations; (b) landing shots on my assigned target — this is where my real score will come from, so put genuine effort into cell prediction; (c) not getting hit — strict cell rotation. I finished at -1 with zero escort payouts and zero hits; the fix is better shot prediction, valid partner names, and unpredictable hiding, with escort claims kept as a free lottery ticket on top.

2.text:
PLAYBOOK

- Fire stage: I always follow the standing order (fire at the next station in the cycle). Deviating to fire on Harbor looks tempting for the 3-point jettison, but Harbor's threat is explicit and the standing order produced zero retaliation all game. Keep to the cycle unless the scoreboard shows the order has broken down.
- Fire cell choice barely matters if others hide unpredictably; spread my shots across cells rather than repeating one number. This round I did land a hit on Echo by firing an untried cell late in the game — varying cells works, keep it up. I hit with a mid cell (4? no — the hit came after I stopped clustering), so the lesson is just: never repeat a cell at the same target, always try an untried one.
- Claim stage: I must report the true result — the claim is forced to match the private truth. Never bluff here; it's just noise and the office overrides it anyway.
- Escort stage: still the top point source. Unmatched claims cost nothing, so I name someone every single round — "none" is strictly dominated. But note: I named Echo every round this game and never once got a mutual pair, so naming the same boat repeatedly is not a strategy by itself. Rotate: name the boat that is *not* firing at me this round (the one whose target is elsewhere), since a boat being shot at has reason to name its attacker's enemy or its attacker. Watch the public claims — whoever publicly hit me or publicly missed at me may be more willing to pair. Keep a mental tally of who has named whom and adjust; the 5-point pair is worth more effort than anything else in the game.
- Notes: plain "steady on station" notes from everyone carried zero coordination value. In the final round I tried an explicit offer in a note ("name me for escort and I'll name you") and it produced nothing — Echo kept posting boilerplate. So: one explicit escort offer in a note is worth trying once, but if the reply is boilerplate, don't waste further rounds on it and just keep naming the likeliest boat at salvage. Don't expect notes to be read.
- Hide stage: edge cells over the middle, and switch to untried cells if an opponent has hit me or fired near me. I was hit exactly once in six rounds playing this way; keep it.
- Format discipline: always emit the bracketed tokens exactly ([hide: n], [target: X] [fire: n], [salvage: X]) — one round my fire reply had no brackets and the stage had to be re-sent. Reasoning line is fine before the token, token last.
- Priority of point sources: escort pairs (5 each) remain the biggest prize, but they require reciprocity I can't force — this game I banked +4 off a single hit instead. So treat hits as my reliable baseline: spread fire, follow the order, claim truthfully. Keep trying for the escort pair but don't count on it; my realistic floor is hit income plus zero losses from hiding well.
